items.title: Tommy Ridgley Interview, 1986-06-20
items.q: See, this was, I had that good band. Justin, Adam, and Emma, we'd go right into things.

ctx.x: Well, getting back, did you ever think of yourself as a rock and roll star? As a rock and roll artist? Yeah, yeah. You did?

Typical, I was a rock and roll artist. See, When I Meet My Girl was defined as the first rockabilly tune to be the hit. You know, because it was a national record. And it was the first rockabilly. And from there, you know, I was strictly rock and roll. See, I played all of the white colleges. What could we talk about? I played from here, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. I played all of them. And it was strictly, you know, rock and roll. We did some of the, like, What I Say, Oop-Oop-A-Doo, was the tunes. But,…
Well, when we were on that, I have a note here about, how did you all travel when you were on the road? How did you, in those days?

items.title: Tommy Ridgley Interview, 1986-03-22
items.q: I'm talking about my original untouchable. That was me, Justin Adams, Dalton Russo, David Francois

ctx.x: Something we haven't really talked about, and we can get back to that, to what you did. What did your parents tell you about whites, about whites, and how to behave?

You know, okay, first of all, I can say this. You see, my family being the type of people that they were, we never did have no white problem. We never had no white. You know what, I think it's because I think being from a decent family, I think we were kind of looked on as just poor, decent people. Now there always was that other kind, that other person, you know, them other people. But my family, we never had no problem. And I say that, to say this, even during the civil rights struggle with me, playing music, I…
You were careful not to talk to anybody?
